messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan, a 34-year-old married South Asian man, had always prided himself on his steady work as a delivery driver, navigating the busy streets of his city with a calm efficiency. That changed thirteen months ago, on a Tuesday afternoon that now felt permanently etched into his memory. He had been running slightly behind schedule, a rare occurrence, and in a moment of hurried distraction at an intersection, he failed to see a cyclist merging into the lane. The impact was sickening, and the image of the cyclist lying on the pavement, groaning in pain with a clearly broken leg, became the anchor for everything that followed. The police report cleared him of gross negligence, attributing it to an unfortunate accident, but Rohan’s internal verdict was far harsher.

From that day, a pervasive sense of self-reproach settled deep within him. He was certain that the event happened because of the way he acted, replaying the scenario countless times in his mind. Each time, he saw himself making a different choice, a split-second decision that could have averted the collision entirely. He believed he should have protected the cyclist, and he felt a profound, aching failure that he hadn't. That feeling of failing to protect another person, a stranger simply going about their day, became a constant companion. He would often find himself staring blankly ahead, consumed by the conviction that he had let someone down in the most fundamental way, a conviction that never seemed to lessen in intensity.

What haunted Rohan most was the relentless thought that he could have done more. He would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened. He was convinced that if only he had been more vigilant, if only he had slowed down just a fraction more, if only he had checked his blind spot one last time, the accident would not have occurred. This inaction guilt was a heavy burden, making it difficult to focus on anything else. During his long shifts behind the wheel of his delivery van, traversing the same streets day in and day out, these thoughts would cycle relentlessly. He’d grip the steering wheel, his knuckles white, as the memory of the cyclist’s fall flashed before his eyes, each time accompanied by the piercing internal accusation that it was his fault, his responsibility. The familiar routes, once a source of quiet routine, now felt like a labyrinth of his own mistakes, each turn a reminder of his perceived failure.

He knew his wife, Priya, worried about him. She tried to offer comfort, reminding him of the police findings and the cyclist’s eventual recovery, but her words couldn't penetrate the wall of his self-condemnation. Rohan was convinced that the event happened because of the way he acted, and no external absolution could truly alleviate that internal judgment. The idea that he had directly caused another person's serious injury was a wound that refused to heal, festering into a core belief about his own culpability. He frequently found himself caught in a loop of thinking, "I should have protected others and I failed." This was not just a passing thought; it was a deeply ingrained appraisal of his character and actions, defining his perception of himself since the accident.

The cumulative weight of these self-critical thoughts brought Rohan to seek help. He was tired of living with the constant internal monologue of blame and regret. He wanted to understand why these appraisals had become so entrenched, why he couldn't shake the unwavering conviction that he alone was responsible for the accident and its consequences. He longed for a way to break free from the relentless cycle of "I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened," a sentiment that overshadowed every aspect of his life, making each day a struggle against his own mind. He hoped therapy could offer some path toward internal peace, though he wasn’t sure such a thing was even possible for someone who felt he had failed so profoundly.
